agent_notes: In the Hebrew text the superscription is verse 1 (KJV 3:0, unnumbered); every later verse is one higher than the KJV. I translated the heading as a verse. The heading is a later editorial note, not part of David's speech; the dramatic layer renders it as a spoken title.

בְּבָרְחוֹ: STEPBible has 'when fled he'; I glossed 'in his fleeing' (infinitive with prefix and suffix). The commentary on the Berakhot 7b tradition (Rashi, Radak) is paraphrased from the packet, not quoted.

history.note: [consider] Consider 'A psalm of David, from the time he fled ...' so the dramatic layer does not settle a question the commentary leaves open. (PS.3.1, Radak: "המזמורים לא היו נקראים בשעת מעשה ... אלא לאחר שנצל מכלם")

agent_notes: יְשׁוּעָתָה: STEPBible glosses it as a plain noun. I kept the archaic -ah ending visible in the commentary (Ibn Ezra and Radak both treat it as an emphatic or doubled form). 'Selah' is left untranslated in all layers; its sense is disputed among Ibn Ezra, Radak and Meiri, as the commentary notes.

בַּעֲדִי: the sources split. KJV 'for me' (on my behalf), ASV 'about me', STEPBible 'behind me', Metzudat Zion 'facing me' (kenegdi). I kept 'about me' in the literal layer and the dramatic layer's 'wrapped around me' as my preference, and the commentary now says so instead of presenting it as a correction of the KJV.

history.note: [should_fix] Rewrite the ba'ad sentence so it agrees with the note and the sources: ba'ad can mean 'for, on behalf of' (KJV) and also 'around, behind' (ASV 'about me'; STEPBible 'behind me'), and Metzudat Zion reads 'facing me'. The 'surrounding shield' image is then a preference, not a correction of the KJV. (PS.3.4: "מָגֵן בַּעֲדִי"; STEPBible gloss "behind me"; Metzudat Zion: "בעדי. כנגדי"; ASV "a shield about me")

agent_notes: וַיַּעֲנֵנִי is a wayyiqtol (narrative past) after a yiqtol 'I call'. Radak and Meiri read it as past-for-future (prophetic perfect). I rendered it as a plain 'and he answers me' in the literal layer to keep the tense ambiguity open, and 'he answers' in the dramatic layer. Alternative: 'he answered me'.

וָאִישָׁנָה: STEPBible parses it as a cohortative-shaped wayyiqtol with a paragogic he. I glossed 'and I slept' with the emphatic nuance in the note. The Hebrew has no 'me' after 'laid', so the KJV 'laid me down' is an archaism, not a reflexive in the Hebrew.

history.note: [consider] Either present the 'deliberate act' sense as a guess or drop it, and give the commentators' readings: secure sleep (Radak, Meiri), or sleep weighed down by worry (Rashi, Metzudat David). (PS.3.6, Radak: "שכבתי בבטח ואישן בשלום"; Rashi: "לִבִּי אָטוּם בִּדְאָגָה וָפַחַד")

agent_notes: שָׁתוּ: Rashi's first reading derives it from שְׁאִיָּה 'desolation' (Isa 24:12), 'they laid waste'; he gives 'set' (like שָׂמוּ, Exod 10:1) only as a second opinion. 'Set their faces to fight me' is Metzudat David. The Isa 22:7 and Job 38:11 parallels are cited by Radak and Meiri; Metzudat Zion adds Ps 73:9. I follow the 'set' reading, which Radak, Meiri, Metzudat David and Metzudat Zion share.

history.note: [should_fix] In the commentary, credit 'they set their faces (to fight me)' to Metzudat David, and say that Rashi gives 'set' only as a second opinion after his reading 'laid waste' (from שְׁאִיָּה). In the שָׁתוּ note, take Rashi off the list that cites Isa 22:7 and Job 38:11, which leaves Radak, Meiri and Metzudat Zion. (PS.3.7, Rashi: "שָׁתוּ. לְשׁוֹן ״שְׁאִיָּה״ ... וְיֵשׁ אוֹמְרִים: שָׁתוּ כְּמוֹ שָׂמוּ"; Metzudat David: "אשר שמו פניהם להלחם בי"; Metzudat Zion: "שתו. שמו")

agent_notes: כִּי הִכִּיתָ: the perfect after a petition can be read as a past (God has done this before, so do it now: Radak, Meiri, Metzudat David) or as a prophetic perfect (it is already done). The English versions split too (all take it as past). I chose the reading 'for you have struck', which leaves both open. I could not trace the claim in Radak that every other 'קומה' in Psalms is accented on the last syllable beyond the packet's own wording; I left it out of the commentary.

לֶחִי: KJV and ASV 'cheek bone' is the old word for jaw; BBE 'face-bones'. The Hebrew is the jaw or cheek, and the blow is a public insult (Lam 3:30; Mic 4:14, cited by Rashi and Metzudat David). I stayed with 'jaw'.

history.note: [consider] Credit both readings to Radak, and the past reading to Meiri and Metzudat David. (PS.3.8, Meiri: "כי כמה הושעתני והכית את כל אויבי בלחי"; Radak: "פעמים רבות הושעתני ... או פרושו על זאת המלחמה")

agent_notes: The verse has no verb in Hebrew: 'to YHWH the deliverance; on your people your blessing'. Translators supply 'belongeth' and 'is' (or a wish: ASV 'be'). I put the supplied words in brackets; the dramatic layer reads it as an assertion, not a wish. The yeshuʿah echo points back to verse 3; the superscription (verse 1) does not contain the word.
